domain_label: Agency Models, Host Agencies & Niche Selection
purpose: How a travel advisor decides the structural shape of the practice - host-agency affiliation versus independent accreditation, which registration and insurance-licensing obligation classes must be verified before selling, which niche of destination, trip type and clientele the practice will concentrate in, and whether income comes from supplier commission, client-paid planning fees or a hybrid - and how those four choices constrain each other, set the practice's supplier leverage and referral surface, and determine what must be disclosed to clients about how the advisor is paid.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors

the practice is a small independent travel advisory business - one advisor or a handful of independent contractors - not a corporate travel management company, tour operator or wholesaler buying inventory at net

commission rates, host-agency splits, consortium dues, planning-fee levels and supplier bonus programs vary by supplier, host, product, region and contract year; every one of them is treated here as a mechanism to read out of your own contract and verify per deal, never as a fixed figure

registration, bonding, trust-account and insurance-licensing requirements differ by state, province and country and change over time; this KB names the obligation class to check and the verification act, and never asserts what a specific jurisdiction currently requires
the advisor works with leisure and independent clients who can walk away, compare online, and talk to each other - so pricing honesty and disclosure are commercial mechanics, not just compliance
this is educational operating knowledge for running the practice, not personalized legal, tax, financial or insurance advice for any advisor or client
exclusions: client discovery sessions, itinerary design and the craft of building a trip - that is the trip-design KB this one hands the model, niche and fee rules to
supplier selection at booking time, reservation mechanics, documentation, payment handling and in-trip disruption advocacy - trip-design and supplier-management KB territory
commission tracking, booked-versus-traveled payment timing, chasing unpaid commission, and planning-fee collection mechanics - the commissions and repeat-client KB owns those
travel-protection and insurance product comparison, add-on presentation scripts, and the post-trip follow-up, anniversary and referral cadence engine - commissions and repeat-client KB territory
naming specific host agencies, consortia, franchise brands or suppliers, and quoting any split percentage, commission rate, membership fee or planning-fee amount as fact

jurisdiction-specific legal conclusions: exact registration thresholds, bond amounts, trust-account rules, license names or exemptions - those are named as classes to verify with the regulator, never stated
corporate travel management, group tour operating, and wholesale contracting where inventory is bought at net and resold
personalized financial, tax, legal, medical or insurance recommendations to a specific client or a specific advisor

competency_questions.question: Should this practice operate under a host agency or pursue its own accreditation, and what facts actually decide it rather than preference?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PRACTICE_MODEL_FRAME states which revenue mechanisms the practice runs on, HOST_AGENCY_MODEL and INDEPENDENT_ACCREDITATION_PATH each state what the model supplies and costs as a mechanism, and the decision is tied to booking volume, administrative capacity and support needs rather than to a headline split

competency_questions.question: Which registration and licensing obligation classes must I verify before I advertise, quote or take money for travel, and how do I verify them for my own jurisdiction?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SELLER_OF_TRAVEL_CLASS enumerates the registration, bonding, trust-account and advertising-disclosure classes to check and the verification act with a dated record; INSURANCE_LICENSE_CLASS does the same for offering travel protection; neither asserts a jurisdiction's specific rule

competency_questions.question: What legal, insurance and contract baseline has to exist before the first client hands me money?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ENTITY_AND_EO_BASELINE names the entity decision, the errors-and-omissions coverage class, the three contract surfaces the advisor signs or issues, and the client-money and record-keeping discipline that must be in place first

competency_questions.question: How do I evaluate a specific host agency before signing, and which contract terms decide whether I could ever leave with my clients intact?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HOST_SELECTION_DILIGENCE lists the questions with sourced answers and contract clause references, and MODEL_EXIT_PORTABILITY names what does and does not travel with the advisor at exit and how in-progress bookings are handled

competency_questions.question: For a booking I make tomorrow, where does the commission money physically travel and who touches it before I do?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: COMMISSION_FLOW_STRUCTURE traces the path from supplier to accreditation holder to advisor, states that whose accreditation identifier the booking carries determines who the supplier pays, and distinguishes agency-billed from supplier-direct and merchant-model bookings

competency_questions.question: What does consortium or preferred-program access actually buy my clients, and what duty does joining create toward them?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CONSORTIUM_ACCESS describes preferred-program benefits and production expectations as mechanisms and names access via host versus direct membership, and CONFLICT_DISCLOSURE_RULE states the written disclosure and the non-preferred-alternative rule that participation triggers

competency_questions.question: How do I choose a niche across destination, trip type and clientele, and how do I test it before I build the practice on it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: NICHE_SELECTION_FRAME gives the three axes and the selection criteria, and NICHE_VIABILITY_TEST gives an evidence test covering reachable buyers, bookable commissionable suppliers, fee tolerance, repeat cadence and concentration risk

competency_questions.question: Why does concentrating in a niche change what suppliers will actually do for my clients?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SUPPLIER_LEVERAGE_FROM_NICHE explains recognition, escalation access and program tiering as volume-driven mechanisms, names the client-visible benefit, and states the limit that leverage must never become undisclosed steering

competency_questions.question: Which clients do I serve, which do I decline, and how do I handle an enquiry where the traveler may be vulnerable or is not the person calling me?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CLIENT_PROFILE_AND_DECLINE defines the served profile, the decline criteria and a respectful decline-with-referral script, and ADVICE_BOUNDARY_DUTY_OF_CARE gives the authority, consent, pacing and written-confirmation practices for vulnerable travelers and third-party bookers

competency_questions.question: How does my niche decide who refers me and what words they use, and which credentials are worth buying to support it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: REFERRAL_SURFACE_DESIGN ties the referable one-sentence description and the communities it travels through to the niche, and CREDENTIAL_AND_POSITIONING_STACK sequences credential purchase after viability evidence and forbids claiming expertise not actually held

competency_questions.question: Should I charge planning fees or work commission-only, and what does each choice do to my alignment with the client and to the work I can afford to accept?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FEE_MODEL_DESIGN states what the fee buys, when it is charged, whether it is credited, and how each option changes the advisor's incentive relative to product choice; NONCOMMISSIONABLE_WORK_POLICY states the written rule for work that pays no commission

competency_questions.question: What exactly must I disclose to a client about how I am paid and about my preferred-supplier relationships, and when must I say it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CONFLICT_DISCLOSURE_RULE names every incentive source that can tilt a recommendation, requires written disclosure before the client commits money, and requires a non-preferred alternative alongside any preferred recommendation with the reason for the recommendation recorded

competency_questions.question: What do I say to a client who has found the same hotel cheaper online and asks why they should book through me?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PRICE_EXPECTATION_HONESTY separates what an advisor can genuinely change about price and inclusions from what they cannot, forbids any always-cheaper claim, and states what the client is actually buying when the rate is identical

competency_questions.question: Can the model, niche and fee combination I have chosen actually carry my fixed costs and my working hours, and how do I check that with my own numbers?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PRACTICE_CAPACITY_ECONOMICS gives the hours-per-trip-type by trips-per-period by fixed-cost structure as a computation the advisor performs on their own contract terms, and ties the result to intake limits and fee floors rather than to any published average

glossary.definition: An agency that holds industry accreditation and supplier relationships and lets affiliated independent advisors book under them, providing back office, supplier support, training and often consortium access, in exchange for a fee structure and a share of the commission set by the affiliation contract.

The contract between an advisor and a host agency that sets the fee and commission split, what support is provided, who owns client data, what happens to in-progress bookings, and the notice and non-solicitation terms that govern departure; it is the single document that most determines the advisor's leverage.

The industry number issued to an accredited agency that suppliers use to recognize the seller and route commission; a booking made under a host's identifier is a booking the supplier pays the host, which is why whose identifier appears on a reservation determines the whole commission path.

A buying and marketing group that agencies join, whether directly or through a host, to gain negotiated preferred-supplier programs, client amenities, marketing tools and supplier access; membership typically carries dues and production expectations set by contract.

A supplier relationship negotiated by a host or consortium that can carry client-facing amenities and advisor-facing commercial terms; because it creates an incentive to recommend one supplier over another, participation is what makes written compensation disclosure a duty rather than a courtesy.

The category of obligation - registration, bonding or surety, trust or escrow handling of client funds, and disclosure of a registration number in advertising - that some jurisdictions impose on anyone selling travel; whether it applies, and to whom, must be verified with the relevant regulator before selling.

The category of licensing and insurer-appointment obligation that can attach to selling, soliciting or advising on travel protection products; some jurisdictions permit narrow unlicensed activity and others do not, so the class and its current boundaries must be verified before any protection product is offered.

The contractual division of a supplier-paid commission between the accreditation holder and the advisor who made the booking; splits commonly vary by product, by annual production tier and by which support services the advisor uses, so the split is read from the contract per booking type rather than assumed.

A fee the client pays the advisor directly for discovery, research, itinerary design and advocacy, charged as a consultation fee, a design or research fee, a per-booking service fee or a retainer; it is the mechanism that decouples advisor income from which product the client eventually buys.

A supplier-, host- or consortium-sponsored trip that lets an advisor inspect properties and destinations firsthand; it builds genuine product knowledge and supplier relationships, and it is also a benefit flowing from a supplier, which is why it belongs in the advisor's disclosure inventory.

nodes.definition: Write down, before any client work, what this practice actually sells and by which mechanism each unit of revenue comes into existence, because the phrase travel agent covers at least three different businesses. The frame names the revenue mechanisms available to a leisure advisory practice - supplier commission paid to whoever holds the accreditation the booking was made under, a fee the client pays the advisor directly for planning and advocacy, and commission on protection or add-on products where the requirement class permits offering them - and states which of them the practice intends to lean on first and why. It also states the negative: whether the practice buys inventory at net and resells it (a tour operator, a different business with different obligations), whether it handles corporate travel programs, and which categories of request it will simply not take. The frame is the reference every later decision is checked against: a host-versus-independent choice, a niche, a fee schedule and an intake limit are only right or wrong relative to a stated revenue mechanism, and an advisor who never wrote one ends up defending each decision on instinct.

included: the revenue mechanisms this practice will run on
advisory-versus-transaction positioning
categories of work the practice explicitly will not take
excluded: how a trip is designed for a specific client
which supplier is chosen for a given booking

pros.claim: Naming the revenue mechanism first makes every downstream decision checkable against something instead of against instinct
pros.example: an advisor who has written that planning fees carry the practice can decline an unpaid air-only reshuffle without agonising over it for a week

pros.claim: Stating what the practice will not sell prevents drifting into a business with different licensing and inventory obligations
pros.example: declining to assemble and resell a packaged group departure at a marked-up net rate, which would put the practice in tour-operator territory

cons.claim: A frame written before any real client contact encodes assumptions about demand that the local market may simply not confirm
cons.example: committing to a fee-first practice in a circle whose first enquiries are all cruise buyers who expect the booking to cost them nothing extra

cons.claim: A tightly written frame can make an advisor refuse early work that would have taught them what their market actually wants
cons.example: turning away three small hotel-only bookings that would have revealed a repeatable corporate-relocation pattern

failure_modes: describing the practice as helping people travel without naming a single mechanism by which money arrives
assuming supplier commission alone will fund advisory-depth work on trips that take many hours to design
copying another advisor's public model without checking whether the same client base exists within reach
acceptance_tests: the frame names each revenue mechanism the practice will use, states who pays it and by what act it comes into existence, and lists at least two categories of work the practice will refuse
every later structural decision in this KB can be traced back to a mechanism named in the frame
revisit_triggers: the first cohort of real enquiries consistently rejects the stated revenue mechanism
a product category the frame relied on for commission stops paying advisors
the advisor begins doing substantial work that the frame does not describe

base.update_signal: the mix of revenue actually collected over the first serving season differs from the mechanism the frame said the practice would run on

nodes.definition: Establish which travel-seller registration obligation classes apply to this practice before advertising, quoting or accepting any client payment, and record how each was verified and when. The classes to go looking for - not a rule, because these differ by jurisdiction and are amended - include whether the state, province or country operates a seller-of-travel or travel-agency registration regime at all; whether the obligation attaches to where the advisor sits, where the client sits, or where the sale is made, since an advisor working from one state for clients in another may face two regimes; whether client funds must be held in trust or escrow, or covered by a bond, surety or a restitution fund contribution; whether a registration number must appear in advertising, quotes and confirmations; whether charging a planning fee changes the analysis; and whether operating under a host agency's registration covers the affiliated advisor or leaves an independent duty. The work unit is the verification act itself: identify the regulator, read the current requirement from that regulator's own publication, write down what was found with the date and the source, and repeat whenever the practice starts serving a new jurisdiction. This KB never states what any jurisdiction requires - verify current rules in your jurisdiction with the regulator or a qualified professional.

included: the obligation classes to check
which jurisdiction's regime may attach
the dated verification record and its re-check trigger
whether host affiliation covers the advisor
excluded: any specific threshold, bond amount or fee for any named jurisdiction
insurance-selling licensure, which is its own class

pros.claim: Verifying the class before advertising avoids building an offer and a website that must be pulled down or rewritten
pros.example: discovering before launch that a registration number may have to appear in advertising, so the site is built once rather than retrofitted

pros.claim: A dated verification record turns a compliance question into a repeatable check the advisor can re-run each year
pros.example: a one-page register listing the regulator, the requirement checked, the source consulted and the date, re-opened every renewal season

cons.claim: Verification takes real time and can stall a launch while the advisor waits for a regulator's answer
cons.example: several weeks lost waiting on a written clarification about whether client-paid planning fees fall inside a client-funds rule

cons.claim: Reading obligations without professional help can produce an over-cautious reading that suppresses legitimate business
cons.example: declining out-of-state clients entirely because a rule looked broader than it was

failure_modes: assuming the host agency's registration automatically covers the affiliated advisor without reading the contract or the rule
checking only the advisor's home jurisdiction and ignoring where clients are located
treating a forum post or another advisor's summary as the source instead of the regulator's own publication
verifying once at launch and never re-checking as rules change
acceptance_tests: for each jurisdiction the practice sells into, the register names the regulator consulted, the obligation classes checked, the date of the check and the source used
the record states explicitly whether host affiliation was found to cover the obligation or not, with the contract clause or rule reference that supports the answer
revisit_triggers: the practice takes a client resident in a jurisdiction not already on the register
the host agency changes its registration status or its coverage language
the practice starts charging a fee type it did not charge when the check was made

base.update_signal: a regulator publishes an amended requirement, or the practice begins selling into a jurisdiction whose regime has not yet been verified

nodes.definition: Determine, before any travel-protection product is offered, quoted or recommended, which licensing and appointment obligation classes attach to that activity for this practice. The classes to check include whether a limited-lines travel insurance producer licence or equivalent is required to sell or solicit protection products; whether an appointment with the specific insurer is required in addition to the licence; whether the host agency or a third-party program holds the licence and the advisor operates under it, and exactly what that permits the advisor to do and say; what narrow activity, if any, an unlicensed person may perform - typically handing over the insurer's own materials, stating that protection exists and referring the client to a licensed party - versus what is restricted, such as comparing policies, interpreting coverage, or advising that a plan suits the client's situation; and whether continuing-education or renewal duties attach. The operating discipline that follows is as important as the licence question: never answer a coverage-interpretation question from memory, route it to the policy wording and the insurer or licensed party, and never use fear to sell protection. Requirements differ by jurisdiction and change - verify current rules in your jurisdiction before offering, and keep the answer dated.

included: licensing and insurer-appointment obligation classes
what unlicensed activity may and may not include
how host or program licensure changes the advisor's permitted acts
the no-fear-selling and route-to-the-policy rules
excluded: comparing or recommending specific protection products, which the commissions and add-ons KB covers
any statement about what a policy covers
naming a licence or insurer or asserting a jurisdiction's rule

pros.claim: Knowing the boundary lets the advisor raise protection with every client without straying into restricted advice
pros.example: saying that protection exists, that pre-existing-condition timing rules are common, and that the insurer or a licensed colleague will answer coverage questions - without interpreting anything

pros.claim: A written boundary protects the client from confident answers the advisor is not qualified to give
pros.example: declining to confirm that a cancellation reason will be covered and sending the client the policy wording and the insurer's line instead

cons.claim: Operating strictly inside the boundary can feel unhelpful to a client who wants a straight answer now
cons.example: a client asking whether a hurricane will be covered and hearing a referral rather than a yes

cons.claim: Licensing and appointment work carries cost and renewal effort that a small practice may not recover from add-on volume alone
cons.example: carrying an annual licence and continuing-education burden while offering protection to a modest number of trips

failure_modes: interpreting coverage for a client because the answer seemed obvious
assuming the host's programme licence permits the advisor to recommend a plan when it may only permit offering materials
using worst-case stories to pressure a hesitant traveler into buying protection
offering protection in a new jurisdiction without re-checking the class
acceptance_tests: the record states which licensing and appointment classes were checked, with the regulator or insurer source and the date, and whether the practice sells, offers under another party's licence, or refers only
a written script exists defining exactly what the advisor may say about protection and where every coverage question is routed
revisit_triggers: the host or programme changes its licensing arrangement or its permitted-activity language
the practice begins offering protection to clients in a new jurisdiction
a client complaint or query reveals the advisor answered a coverage question directly

base.update_signal: a regulator or insurer restates what unlicensed or programme-covered advisors may do, or the practice changes how protection reaches its clients

nodes.definition: Put the practice's legal and contractual floor in place before the first client payment: the business entity decision and its registration, the errors-and-omissions coverage class and what it is expected to respond to, and the three contract surfaces every advisor lives on. Those surfaces are the affiliation contract the advisor signs with a host (or the accreditation and supplier agreements an independent signs), the engagement terms the advisor issues to the client covering scope of service, fees, cancellation and the limits of the advisor's role, and the supplier terms the client is actually buying under, which the advisor passes through rather than authors. Alongside them sits the client-money and record discipline: how client payments reach the supplier, what the advisor may and may not hold or store, how card details are handled, and what record of each engagement is kept and for how long. The unit is complete when an advisor can say, for a hypothetical dispute, which document governs, who carries the coverage, and where the evidence of what was agreed lives. Entity form, coverage and record-retention duties vary by jurisdiction and by contract - verify with a qualified professional rather than adopting another advisor's setup.

included: entity and coverage classes to establish
the affiliation, engagement and supplier contract surfaces
client-money handling and record-retention discipline

pros.claim: Knowing which document governs turns a client dispute from a panic into a lookup
pros.example: a change-penalty argument resolved by pointing to the supplier's own terms and the engagement letter's stated scope

pros.claim: Written engagement terms set the scope of service before expectations form around it
pros.example: stating that the advisor arranges and advocates but does not guarantee supplier performance, before a client assumes otherwise

cons.claim: Setting up entity, coverage and documents costs money and time before a single commission has arrived
cons.example: paying for coverage and document preparation during a first season with a thin booking pipeline

cons.claim: Templates copied from other advisors can conflict with the host contract the advisor has already signed
cons.example: engagement terms promising a refund path the affiliation contract does not permit

failure_modes: taking client money before engagement terms exist, then arguing about scope after a problem
assuming a host's coverage extends to the advisor's own acts without reading what it responds to
storing client card details in an ad-hoc note or message thread
keeping no durable record of what was recommended and what the client chose
acceptance_tests: for a hypothetical dispute the advisor can name the governing document, the coverage that would respond, and where the evidence of the agreement is stored
engagement terms state scope, fees, cancellation and the limits of the advisor's role, and do not contradict the affiliation contract
revisit_triggers: the affiliation contract is amended or the advisor changes host
the practice starts a new service type not described in the engagement terms
a claim, chargeback or complaint exposes a gap between documents

base.update_signal: a dispute, chargeback or coverage question reveals that no document in the stack governs the situation

nodes.definition: Hold a hard line between the travel guidance this practice gives and the licensed advice it must not give, and apply extra care when the traveler may be vulnerable or is not the person on the phone. The boundary in daily practice: entry, visa and documentation requirements are pointed to at the authoritative government or consular source rather than recalled from memory, health precautions are routed to a travel-health professional, protection coverage questions go to the policy wording and a licensed party, and anything financial, tax or legal goes to the client's own professional. The duty-of-care half concerns who is actually deciding: when an adult child books for a parent, when a traveler shows signs of confusion, fatigue or memory difficulty, when a client is making an unusually large commitment relative to what they have said about their means, or when a medical condition will shape the itinerary, the advisor slows down, confirms who has authority to commit funds, gets the traveler's own confirmation where possible, avoids urgency and scarcity pressure, and puts the material terms in writing so the traveler can read them without a voice in their ear. This is a first-class operating rule of the practice, not an ethical footnote.

included: the educational-versus-licensed-advice line and the routing rule for each question type
authority and consent checks for third-party bookers
pacing, written confirmation and anti-pressure practice with vulnerable travelers
excluded: specific entry or health requirements for any destination
in-trip medical or emergency response procedure

pros.claim: Routing licensed questions to the right source protects the traveler and keeps the advisor inside their competence
pros.example: sending a client to the destination government's own entry page for passport validity and visa rules instead of quoting a remembered rule

pros.claim: Written confirmation and a slower pace protect a vulnerable traveler and also protect the advisor if the family later questions the booking
pros.example: emailing the full non-refundable terms to an eighty-year-old traveler and waiting for their own reply before taking a deposit

cons.claim: The routing discipline can read as evasive to a client who wanted the advisor to just answer
cons.example: a client hearing check the consulate's page when they hoped for a yes on a visa-on-arrival question

cons.claim: Extra confirmation steps slow bookings and can cost held inventory in a fast-moving sale
cons.example: losing a limited-cabin hold while waiting for the traveler themselves, not their son, to confirm in writing

failure_modes: answering a visa, health or coverage question from memory because it seemed simple
taking a large deposit from a third party without confirming authority or informing the traveler
using scarcity or fear to move a hesitant or confused traveler to a decision
leaving the material terms of a non-refundable commitment in a phone call with no written trace
acceptance_tests: each licensed or authoritative question type has a named routing destination the advisor uses instead of answering
for third-party or potentially vulnerable bookings there is a recorded authority check, the traveler's own confirmation where obtainable, and written material terms sent before money is taken
revisit_triggers: a client or family member disputes what was understood at the time of booking
the practice begins serving a client group where third-party booking is the norm
the licensing class governing what the advisor may say about protection changes

base.update_signal: a complaint, family objection or regulator guidance shows the boundary or the consent practice was too loose for the clients actually being served

nodes.definition: Understand the host-agency model as a trade of margin for infrastructure, and be able to state exactly what is being bought. A host holds the industry accreditation and the supplier agreements, so bookings the affiliated advisor makes are written under the host's identifier; the supplier pays the host, and the host pays the advisor according to the contracted split. What the affiliation typically supplies, all of which must be confirmed contract by contract, is the accreditation itself, supplier relationships and support desks the advisor could not open alone, commission tracking and disbursement, booking and back-office systems, training and mentorship, marketing tools, sometimes errors-and-omissions coverage on the host's programme, and frequently consortium membership the advisor could not afford directly. What it costs is expressed as some combination of a recurring affiliation fee, a per-booking fee and a share of commission, often varying by product type and annual production tier - mechanisms to read out of the contract, never a figure to assume. The structural consequences matter as much as the money: the host's contract governs how the client relationship is treated, and the host's service level becomes the advisor's service level on the day a client is stranded.

included: what affiliation supplies and how it is charged as mechanisms
the structural consequence of booking under another party's accreditation
when the model fits a starting or low-volume practice
excluded: comparing named hosts or their terms

pros.claim: Affiliation converts a large fixed setup into a variable cost that scales with bookings, which is what makes a first year survivable
pros.example: an advisor selling a handful of trips in the first months without carrying accreditation, systems and supplier onboarding alone

pros.claim: The host's supplier relationships and support desk give a new advisor escalation power they have not personally earned yet
pros.example: a host support desk reaching a supplier contact during a schedule collapse that an unknown independent could not reach

cons.claim: The split reduces yield on every booking for as long as the affiliation lasts, including on business the advisor sourced entirely alone
cons.example: a repeat client who came by referral still generating a shared commission years into the relationship

cons.claim: Booking under another party's accreditation means their contract terms, technology and service levels bound the advisor's practice
cons.example: a host system outage during a peak booking window that the advisor can do nothing about

failure_modes: choosing a host on the headline split alone and discovering the fee structure and support limits afterwards
assuming the host's registration or coverage extends to the advisor without verifying it
treating host-supplied training as a substitute for building genuine product knowledge
letting the host's brand rather than the advisor's own positioning define the practice to clients
acceptance_tests: the advisor can list, from the contract, every service the affiliation supplies and every charge that applies, with the product types where the terms differ
the record states whether the host's registration and coverage extend to the advisor's own acts, with the clause reference
revisit_triggers: the host changes its fee schedule, split tiers or included services
annual booking volume approaches the point where independence would cost less than the split
a support failure during a live client disruption reveals the service level is not what was sold

base.update_signal: the host amends its fee, split or service terms, or the advisor's own volume changes which side of the trade is favourable

nodes.definition: Evaluate the independent path as the mirror image of affiliation: the practice obtains its own industry accreditation, applies for supplier appointments directly, carries its own errors-and-omissions coverage, runs its own booking and accounting systems, and receives supplier commission without a split. What replaces the split is a set of fixed and administrative costs the advisor now owns outright - accreditation and any bonding or registration obligations, coverage, technology, consortium dues if joined directly, and the unglamorous labour of reconciling every commission and chasing the ones that do not arrive. The decision is a threshold computation the advisor performs with their own numbers, never with a published rule of thumb: total the split value given up over a realistic year of bookings, total the fixed and time costs of standing alone, and see which side wins at the volume actually being produced, with a margin for the year being worse than expected. Independence also changes standing with suppliers: appointments must be earned rather than inherited, and a new independent agency has no production history to point at. The path suits a practice with steady volume, administrative appetite, and enough product depth to hold its own with suppliers.

included: what independence requires the practice to own
the threshold computation done on the advisor's own figures
the loss of inherited supplier standing and how it is rebuilt
excluded: specific accreditation programmes, dues or bonding amounts
which suppliers to seek appointments with

pros.claim: Keeping the full commission and owning the supplier relationships raises yield and removes a counterparty from the payment path
pros.example: an established advisor whose steady annual production had been surrendering a share of every booking to a host that supplied little they still used

pros.claim: Owning the accreditation, client data and systems removes the exit risk that affiliation carries
pros.example: no notice period, non-solicitation clause or client-ownership argument standing between the practice and its own book

cons.claim: Fixed costs and administrative labour arrive whether or not the bookings do, and they land on the advisor's own time
cons.example: a slow season where accreditation, coverage and system costs continue while commission does not

cons.claim: A new independent agency starts with no production history, so supplier appointments and programme access must be earned from zero
cons.example: being declined a preferred programme tier that the previous host had made routine

failure_modes: going independent on the strength of the split saved without costing the administrative hours it adds
underestimating commission reconciliation labour and leaving money uncollected
losing consortium and preferred access on exit without a plan to replace it
timing the switch in the middle of a booking-heavy season
acceptance_tests: the threshold computation exists in writing using the practice's own volume, its own contract split and its own quoted fixed costs, with a downside year modelled
the plan names how supplier appointments, programme access and commission reconciliation will be handled from day one of independence
revisit_triggers: booking volume moves materially in either direction from the level used in the threshold computation
a host renegotiation changes the split or fee that the computation assumed
accreditation, bonding or coverage requirements change the fixed-cost side

base.update_signal: a full year of actual production and actual administrative hours proves the threshold computation optimistic or pessimistic

nodes.definition: Run a structured diligence pass on each candidate host and answer every question from the contract and from current affiliates rather than from the recruitment page. The questions that decide the outcome: how the fee and split are structured and what moves them, including whether they differ by product type and by annual production tier; what the recurring and per-booking charges buy and what is charged separately; whether the advisor can see a per-booking commission ledger and how disputes about a missing payment are handled; how quickly and by what channel a live disruption reaches a human, including outside business hours; which supplier relationships and consortium memberships come with affiliation and which do not; what training, mentorship and community actually exist as opposed to a library of recordings; what errors-and-omissions arrangement exists and what it responds to; who owns client data and what the non-solicitation and notice terms say; and what happens to bookings already deposited if the advisor leaves. The diligence artifact is a comparison sheet where each answer carries its source - a contract clause, a written reply from the host, or a named affiliate reference - because recruitment claims and contract language routinely diverge, and the contract is what will be enforced.

included: the diligence question set and its sourcing rule
reading fee, split, support, data-ownership and exit terms from the contract
reference conversations with current and former affiliates

pros.claim: Sourcing each answer to a clause or a named affiliate stops a recruitment claim from becoming an assumption the practice is built on
pros.example: a promised round-the-clock support line that the contract described only as best-effort during business hours

pros.claim: Former affiliates reveal the failure behaviour that current affiliates and marketing never show
pros.example: learning from a departed advisor how long a commission dispute actually took to resolve

cons.claim: Thorough diligence delays affiliation while enquiries are already arriving and cannot be booked
cons.example: several weeks of contract review and reference calls while a first client's departure window closes

cons.claim: Contract language can be read but its enforcement culture cannot, so diligence gives a partial picture at best
cons.example: an exit clause that reads fairly but has historically been applied restrictively

failure_modes: comparing hosts on split alone and ignoring fee structure, support and exit terms
accepting recruitment-page claims without asking for the clause that supports them
speaking only to affiliates the host selected as references
signing before reading what happens to deposited bookings on departure
acceptance_tests: every answer on the comparison sheet cites a contract clause, a written host reply, or a named affiliate conversation
the sheet explicitly records the fee structure, the per-booking ledger visibility, the support escalation path, the data-ownership term and the exit and in-progress-booking terms for each candidate
revisit_triggers: the host issues an amended contract or fee schedule
a live support or commission failure contradicts a diligence answer
the practice's product mix shifts into a category with different split terms

base.update_signal: lived experience of support, commission handling or contract enforcement contradicts what diligence recorded

nodes.definition: Decide how the practice reaches consortium and preferred-supplier programmes - through a host's membership, through direct membership, or not at all - and understand what that access does in both directions. What it can supply, always to be confirmed against the current programme documents: negotiated client amenities on qualifying bookings, programme rates or added value the advisor cannot obtain as an unaffiliated seller, commercial terms that improve with production, marketing and content tools, supplier training, and access to supplier business development contacts who take the call. What it asks in return is production toward preferred suppliers, participation fees or dues, and adherence to programme marketing rules. The second direction is the one advisors underweight: every preferred relationship creates a reason to recommend one supplier over another that has nothing to do with the client in front of you, so joining a programme is what turns written compensation disclosure from good manners into an obligation of the practice. Access should be evaluated on whether the programme's suppliers actually serve the chosen niche - amenity programmes concentrated in categories the practice never books are dues paid for nothing.

included: routes to programme access and what access supplies as mechanisms
production and dues expectations
the disclosure duty that participation creates
fit between programme suppliers and the practice's niche
excluded: choosing a supplier for a specific booking

pros.claim: Programme membership can put real client-visible value on a booking the advisor could not otherwise offer
pros.example: a qualifying hotel booking that carries breakfast and a property credit the same rate would not include booked direct

pros.claim: Programme supplier contacts turn an anonymous booking into one with a named person to escalate to
pros.example: a business development contact who resolves a room-category error the general reservations line would not

cons.claim: Production expectations and dues create pressure to steer bookings toward programme suppliers regardless of fit
cons.example: a preferred property being proposed for a client whose brief clearly pointed to a small non-programme guesthouse

cons.claim: Programme coverage is uneven, so dues can buy value in categories the practice does not sell
cons.example: a rich hotel amenity programme for a practice that books mostly expedition voyages and lodges

failure_modes: joining for the programme list rather than for the suppliers the niche actually uses
letting production targets rather than the client brief select the supplier
presenting a programme amenity as an objective ranking of the property
failing to disclose programme participation in writing before the client commits
acceptance_tests: the access decision records which programme suppliers overlap the practice's niche and what the dues or production expectations are
a written client-facing disclosure of programme participation exists and is delivered before the client commits money
revisit_triggers: programme terms, dues or production expectations change
the practice's niche shifts into supplier categories the programme does not cover
a recommendation is made where the programme benefit and the client brief pull apart

base.update_signal: a season of bookings shows how often programme benefits actually applied to the trips this practice sells

nodes.definition: Be able to draw, for any booking the practice makes, the structural path the money takes and who touches it before the advisor does. The governing fact is that the accreditation identifier on the reservation determines who the supplier recognises as the seller and therefore who the supplier pays: under affiliation that is the host, who then applies the contracted split and disburses to the advisor; standing independently, the supplier pays the practice directly. Layered on top are the booking models, which change who holds the client's money in the first place - the client paying the supplier directly with the advisor's identifier attached, the agency billing the client and remitting net to the supplier, and merchant-model bookings where a third party takes the payment and the commission arrives from them. Different products in the same practice can sit in different models at the same time, and a single itinerary can contain several. What this node deliberately stops at is the calendar: when commission is earned and paid, how it is tracked and chased, and how planning fees are collected belong to the commissions and repeat-client KB. Here the question is only structural - whose identifier, whose money, whose split - because that is what the model choice actually decides.

included: identifier-determines-payee rule
affiliation split path versus direct path
client-direct, agency-billed and merchant booking models as structures
excluded: payment timing, booked-versus-traveled rules, tracking and chasing unpaid commission
any commission percentage or split figure

pros.claim: Knowing whose identifier is on a booking tells the advisor immediately who to ask when money does not appear
pros.example: a supplier confirming payment was issued to the accreditation holder, which redirects the question to the host's ledger rather than the supplier

pros.claim: Recognising which booking model applies prevents the advisor from promising a payment path that does not exist for that product
pros.example: expecting an agency-billed remittance on a product the client paid a merchant platform for directly

cons.claim: The structural map is a static picture that says nothing about whether the money actually arrives on time
cons.example: a correctly drawn path for a booking whose commission still sits unpaid a season after travel

cons.claim: Mixed models inside one itinerary make the structure harder to hold in the advisor's head than a single diagram suggests
cons.example: a trip combining a client-direct voyage deposit, an agency-billed transfer and a merchant-platform hotel night

failure_modes: booking under one accreditation while expecting payment from another party
assuming every product in an itinerary pays through the same path
not knowing whether the client's money passes through the advisor, the host or the supplier
confusing the structural path with the payment calendar and chasing the wrong counterparty
acceptance_tests: for a representative itinerary the advisor can state, per component, which identifier the booking carries, who holds the client's money and who pays the commission to whom
the map names the counterparty to contact first for each component when an expected payment is missing
revisit_triggers: the practice changes model, host or accreditation
a supplier or platform changes how it bills and pays sellers
a new product category enters the practice's mix with an unfamiliar booking model

base.update_signal: a supplier, platform or host changes who is billed and who is paid for a product the practice sells

nodes.definition: Plan the exit before signing the entry, because the terms that decide whether a practice can move are agreed at affiliation and enforced at departure. The inventory to establish in advance: who owns the client records and whether the advisor may export them; what the non-solicitation clause permits the advisor to say to their own past clients after leaving; what notice is required and whether it can be served mid-season; what happens to bookings already deposited under the host's accreditation, including whether commission on trips that travel after departure still pays and to whom; whether supplier appointments, programme access and any specialist designations tied to the host survive the move; whether the advisor's email address, branding and content are theirs or the host's; and whether any residual obligation such as a training-cost repayment or a minimum term applies. The operational half is a transition sequence that protects clients first: existing travelers must never discover a change of arrangements by finding a broken contact path mid-trip, so in-flight bookings are mapped, communicated and shepherded before the practice announces anything. Portability is the single term that most determines whether a book of clients is an asset of the practice or of the host.

included: the portability inventory to settle before signing
treatment of in-progress and post-departure-travel bookings
the client-protective transition sequence
excluded: how to serve clients during a trip disruption

pros.claim: Knowing the exit terms before signing converts a future crisis into a planned move
pros.example: an advisor who timed a departure for the quietest booking window because the notice term was known from the start

pros.claim: A mapped transition protects travelers who are mid-itinerary when the practice changes model
pros.example: every deposited booking assigned a named handling path before any change is announced to clients

cons.claim: Negotiating portability terms at affiliation can cost the advisor leverage or the affiliation itself
cons.example: a host declining to amend a non-solicitation clause for a new advisor with no production history

cons.claim: Even good terms leave a real transition cost in time, systems and client reassurance
cons.example: rebuilding client records in a new system while reassuring travelers who noticed the change of confirmation format

failure_modes: signing without reading what happens to deposited bookings and post-departure travel commission
announcing a move to clients before in-flight bookings are mapped and handled
assuming client records may be exported when the contract says otherwise
leaving during peak season and stranding both clients and the outgoing host
acceptance_tests: the portability inventory is answered in writing from contract clauses before affiliation is signed
any actual transition has a per-booking handling plan for deposited and in-progress travel before a single client is told
revisit_triggers: the affiliation contract is amended, particularly its data, notice or non-solicitation terms
the practice begins seriously evaluating a move
a change in the host's ownership or operating model

base.update_signal: a contract amendment or an actual departure reveals how the portability terms are enforced in practice

nodes.definition: Choose the practice's concentration along three axes that can be combined but should not all be left open: destination (a country, a region, a corridor such as a set of island groups), trip type (multi-generational celebration travel, expedition and small-ship voyages, safari, self-drive touring, dive travel, pilgrimage, culinary or rail journeys), and clientele (a life stage, a profession, an affinity community, an accessibility or dietary requirement). The reason to concentrate is not marketing fashion: a narrow scope is what lets an advisor accumulate genuine product knowledge faster than a generalist, what makes their volume visible to a small set of suppliers, and what gives past clients a sentence they can repeat when someone asks who to use. Selection criteria that hold up: depth of the advisor's own lived and inspected experience, density of bookable commissionable suppliers in the space, whether the buyers can actually be reached through some existing community rather than through general advertising, whether the trips are complex enough that advisory work is genuinely worth paying for, whether the clientele travels again on a rhythm, and how seasonal the space is. The frame states the chosen axes and, importantly, the adjacent work the practice will still take so the choice does not read as a refusal of ordinary business.

included: the three concentration axes and how they combine
selection criteria for a candidate niche
the adjacent work the practice still accepts
excluded: the evidence test that validates the candidate
credential purchases keyed to the niche

pros.claim: Concentration compounds product knowledge far faster than generalist work does, and knowledge is what clients are actually buying
pros.example: an advisor who has personally inspected a dozen lodges in one safari corridor answering a question in a sentence that a generalist would need a week of research to answer

pros.claim: A stated niche gives past clients language to refer with, which is how a small practice grows without advertising
pros.example: a client telling a friend that their advisor only does small-ship expedition voyages, which is repeatable in a way that helps with travel is not

cons.claim: A narrow scope shrinks the addressable enquiry pool at exactly the moment a young practice needs volume
cons.example: declining routine beach-resort enquiries in a first year while waiting for expedition clients to appear

cons.claim: Concentration creates exposure to shocks in a single destination or product category
cons.example: a practice built on one region when that region closes to visitors for a season

failure_modes: choosing a niche from personal enthusiasm with no reachable buyers behind it
picking a niche so broad it changes nothing about how the practice works
stacking all three axes so tightly that almost no real enquiry qualifies
declaring a niche publicly before any evidence that it can be sold
acceptance_tests: the niche statement names the axes chosen, the criteria that justified them, and the adjacent work the practice will still accept
the advisor can name where the buyers for this niche already gather without paid advertising
revisit_triggers: enquiry flow in the niche stays thin after a full seasonal cycle
the practice finds itself repeatedly serving a different profile than the one stated
a destination or product category central to the niche becomes unsellable

base.update_signal: the profile of clients the practice actually books diverges from the niche the frame declared

nodes.definition: Test a candidate niche against evidence before the practice is built around it, using checks an advisor can run in weeks rather than after a lost year. The checks: name the specific places the buyers already gather - a club, an association, an alumni network, a congregation, a school community, an online group with real membership - and confirm the advisor can be present there without buying attention; count the bookable, commissionable suppliers serving the niche and confirm that they pay advisors at all, since some categories are largely direct-sell and some of the most attractive trip types have thin or no commission; run a small number of real conversations with real prospective clients about a real trip, listening for whether they engage with a planning fee or flinch at the word; check the repeat rhythm, since a niche whose travelers go once in a decade builds no base; and check concentration risk by asking what happens to the practice if one destination closes or one supplier withdraws. The test produces a written verdict with the evidence attached, so the eventual decision to commit is traceable to something other than enthusiasm.

included: reachability, supplier density, fee tolerance, repeat rhythm and concentration checks
a small number of real prospect conversations
the written verdict with evidence
excluded: buying credentials keyed to the niche

pros.claim: A few real conversations expose a fee-intolerant or direct-sell niche before the practice reorganises around it
pros.example: learning in three conversations that the community in question books its annual trip through an organiser who already handles it

pros.claim: Counting commissionable suppliers separates a niche that is lovely to talk about from one that pays
pros.example: discovering that a favourite trip type is served mainly by operators who sell direct and pay advisors nothing

cons.claim: A small sample of conversations can mislead in either direction and is not a market study
cons.example: three enthusiastic responses from friends of friends who never become clients

cons.claim: Testing consumes weeks of a starting practice's scarce time before any revenue exists
cons.example: a month spent validating a niche while general enquiries go unanswered

failure_modes: treating social media engagement as evidence of buyers
testing with friends and family whose politeness produces false positives
skipping the commissionable-supplier count and discovering the payment gap after committing
ignoring concentration risk because the current season looks strong
acceptance_tests: the verdict lists named gathering places for buyers, a counted set of commissionable suppliers, the observed reaction to a fee, an assessment of repeat rhythm and a concentration-risk answer
each claim in the verdict is attached to an observation rather than to an assumption
revisit_triggers: an assumption in the verdict is contradicted by real enquiry flow
a major supplier in the niche changes whether or how it pays advisors
the community used to reach buyers changes access rules or leadership

base.update_signal: actual enquiry and booking flow in the niche over a full season contradicts the test verdict

nodes.definition: Understand the mechanism that makes niching commercially real rather than cosmetic: suppliers allocate attention, inventory flexibility and goodwill toward sellers whose production they can see, and a concentrated practice becomes visible to a small set of suppliers far sooner than a scattered one. The visible effects are practical - a business development contact who answers directly, a request for a difficult date that gets worked rather than declined, an accurate answer about a property or vessel from someone who knows it, an invitation to inspection and familiarization travel that turns into real product knowledge, and programme tiers that improve as production accumulates. All of that is a mechanism driven by production and relationship, never a published entitlement, so the practice should describe it as leverage earned per supplier and confirm what each relationship actually provides. Two limits belong inside this node rather than as afterthoughts. First, leverage is only worth having if it converts into something the client can see, such as a resolved problem or a genuine amenity. Second, the pull toward suppliers who reward the advisor must never become undisclosed steering: leverage informs which suppliers the practice can serve well, and disclosure governs how that is presented to the client.

included: the production-to-recognition mechanism
what earned standing looks like operationally
the client-visible test and the anti-steering limit
excluded: choosing the supplier for a specific booking
negotiating rates or contracts with suppliers

pros.claim: Concentrated production earns escalation access that changes outcomes on the day something goes wrong
pros.example: a known contact at a lodge finding a replacement room after an overbooking that a general reservations queue would have refused

pros.claim: Repeat exposure to the same suppliers produces accurate first-hand knowledge instead of brochure knowledge
pros.example: warning a client that a highly rated cabin category sits under a noisy deck because the advisor has slept in it

cons.claim: Earned standing creates a gravitational pull toward the suppliers who reward the advisor, which can distort recommendations
cons.example: reaching first for the operator whose team knows you rather than the one whose itinerary matches the brief

cons.claim: Leverage is personal and non-portable, so it evaporates when a contact leaves or a supplier restructures
cons.example: a business development contact moving on and the practice reverting to an anonymous queue

failure_modes: mistaking hospitality received for leverage that will actually help a client
concentrating so hard on one supplier that the practice cannot serve a brief that supplier does not fit
letting familiarization invitations rather than client outcomes drive the supplier set
presenting a relationship-driven recommendation as an objective comparison
acceptance_tests: for each core supplier the practice can name what standing it has earned and what that standing has actually produced for a client
any recommendation traceable to supplier relationship carries the disclosure and an alternative for the client to weigh
revisit_triggers: a key supplier contact departs or the supplier restructures its trade programme
a client brief repeatedly falls outside the practice's supplier set
an audit of recommendations shows one supplier dominating regardless of brief

base.update_signal: a review of a season's bookings shows whether supplier standing produced client-visible outcomes or only advisor-visible benefits

nodes.definition: Define the client the practice is built to serve and, with equal precision, the enquiries it will decline, because a small advisory practice is capacity-bound and every accepted misfit displaces a fit. The served profile is described in observable terms rather than demographics: the complexity of trip they are planning, their posture toward spending and toward value, how they prefer to decide, how far ahead they plan, whether they want a collaborator or a decision-maker, and whether their expectations of an advisor are compatible with what the practice sells. The decline list is the mirror: enquiries whose budget cannot carry the trip they are describing, requests that are purely price-shopping an already-designed trip, work outside the practice's supplier competence, prospects who want the advisor to underwrite risks no advisor can control, and situations where serving well would require licensed advice the practice cannot give. Declining is itself a skill: it is done early, plainly, without implying the client is at fault, with a referral to someone or something more suitable, and without a fee dangling. Duty of care sits inside this unit too, since some enquiries need slowing down rather than declining.

included: observable served-client profile
explicit decline criteria and the decline-with-referral practice
the slow-down-rather-than-decline case
excluded: the discovery conversation itself and trip design

pros.claim: An explicit decline list converts an uncomfortable judgement call into a policy the advisor can apply calmly in the first conversation
pros.example: recognising a price-shopping enquiry for an already-built itinerary and declining it in the first ten minutes rather than after twelve hours of research

pros.claim: Declining early protects the clients the practice already has from a capacity squeeze
pros.example: keeping the design week clear for a deposited client instead of absorbing a mismatched enquiry

cons.claim: A young practice declining work feels like refusing money, and the profile may be wrong in the first place
cons.example: turning away an out-of-niche enquiry that would have opened an entire community of similar travelers

cons.claim: A profile written in observable terms can still be applied with unconscious bias if the criteria drift toward who the advisor finds comfortable
cons.example: declining enquiries with unfamiliar communication styles under the guise of fit

failure_modes: having no decline criteria and absorbing every enquiry until service quality drops
declining by silence, which damages referrals more than a clear no
using fit language to disguise a decision that is really about budget, without saying so honestly
accepting an enquiry that would require licensed advice the practice cannot give
acceptance_tests: the profile and the decline criteria are written in terms an advisor can observe in a first conversation
every decline in a period was delivered promptly, with a reason the client could act on and a referral or alternative
revisit_triggers: declined enquiries cluster into a pattern the practice could profitably serve
accepted clients repeatedly turn out to be misfits despite meeting the criteria
capacity pressure changes what the practice can responsibly accept

base.update_signal: the pattern of accepted, declined and regretted enquiries over a season shows the criteria are selecting the wrong clients

nodes.definition: Design the structural side of referral: what the practice is known for, who is positioned to repeat it, and where that repetition happens. A referral is a sentence somebody says when a friend mentions a trip, so the practice needs a description short enough to survive being repeated and specific enough to attach to a situation - a trip type, a destination corridor, a life event, a community. The structural work is threefold: make the specialty legible everywhere a prospective client verifies the advisor, so the referred person finds the same claim the referrer made; anchor the practice inside communities where the niche's travelers already talk to each other, whether that is a dive club, an alumni chapter, a congregation, a school parents' group or a professional association, and be present there as a participant rather than an advertiser; and give past clients a natural occasion to mention the practice by being visibly connected to the thing they care about. What this node does not own is the outreach engine - post-trip follow-up, anniversary contact, the referral ask and the cadence of staying in touch belong to the commissions and repeat-client KB. Here the question is only whether the niche and positioning make referrals structurally possible.

included: the repeatable one-sentence description
consistency of the specialty claim across every place a client verifies it
community anchoring where the niche's travelers already gather
excluded: post-trip follow-up, anniversary outreach and referral-ask cadence

pros.claim: A specific, repeatable description travels through a community in a way a general one cannot
pros.example: someone in a dive club saying she books everyone's liveaboard trips, which lands where she is a travel agent would not

pros.claim: Community anchoring puts the practice where the buyers already are, which a small practice can sustain without advertising budget
pros.example: regular participation in an alumni travel group that produces enquiries at every reunion cycle

cons.claim: A tightly framed description filters out adjacent work that past clients would happily have sent
cons.example: a friend not thinking to mention the advisor for a family beach week because they are known only for expedition voyages

cons.claim: Community presence takes sustained personal time and cannot be delegated or switched on when the pipeline is thin
cons.example: months of participation before the first enquiry arrives from a newly joined association

failure_modes: describing the practice differently in each place a client might check it
joining communities purely to prospect, which the community notices and rejects
relying on referrals without a legible specialty for referrers to repeat
confusing structural referability with the follow-up cadence that actually asks
acceptance_tests: the practice has one short description of what it does that a past client could repeat accurately from memory, and it appears consistently everywhere the practice is visible
at least one community where the niche's travelers already gather is named, with the advisor's participating role in it stated
revisit_triggers: referrals arrive describing the practice in words that do not match the stated specialty
the community used as an anchor changes, disperses or closes to participation
the niche is adjusted, which makes the description stale

base.update_signal: the words referrers actually use, and the communities referrals actually come from, differ from the designed surface

nodes.definition: Decide which credential classes are worth the practice's money and time, and hold the line on what may be claimed because of them. The classes available to a travel advisor include supplier and destination certification programmes, cruise and expedition line academies, host- and consortium-run training tracks, and industry association designations; what each actually supplies varies and must be checked before purchase - typically product knowledge, sometimes a listing in a specialist finder that produces enquiries, sometimes access to inspection travel, occasionally commercial or amenity access, and always a badge. The sequencing rule matters more than the choice: credentials are bought after niche viability evidence exists, because a certification keyed to a niche the practice abandons is a sunk cost with a badge attached. The honesty rule is stricter still: a certificate is evidence of completed training, not of having been somewhere or having sold something, and it must never be presented in a way that implies experience the advisor does not have. Where the practice is genuinely new to a destination or product, say so and pair the gap with the supplier relationship or colleague who fills it, since a client discovering an overstated claim mid-trip costs far more than the enquiry it won.

included: credential classes and what each may supply
buy-after-evidence sequencing
the honest-claim rule and how to state a genuine gap
excluded: naming specific programmes, designations or their costs

pros.claim: Some certification programmes place the advisor in a finder that referrers and travelers actually search, producing enquiries the practice would not otherwise see
pros.example: an enquiry arriving through a destination specialist listing from a traveler with no prior connection to the practice

pros.claim: Structured product training compresses the time it takes to speak accurately about a niche's suppliers
pros.example: learning the real differences between vessel classes before a client asks rather than during the conversation

cons.claim: Credentials are easy to accumulate and easy to mistake for demand, and the badge does not sell trips by itself
cons.example: a wall of completed certificates in a niche that has produced two enquiries all year

cons.claim: A badge can imply firsthand experience the advisor lacks, and clients discover the gap at the worst possible moment
cons.example: a certified destination specialist unable to answer a basic on-the-ground logistics question during trip planning

failure_modes: buying certifications before testing whether the niche can be sold
presenting completed training as personal travel experience
collecting designations that produce no enquiries and no knowledge the practice uses
hiding a genuine experience gap instead of pairing it with a supplier or colleague who covers it
acceptance_tests: each credential the practice holds is tied to a stated purpose - knowledge, listing, access - and to the niche the viability test validated
every public claim of expertise can be substantiated by training completed, trips designed or places actually visited, with gaps stated plainly
revisit_triggers: a credential produces no enquiries, knowledge or access over a full renewal cycle
the practice's niche changes
a client question exposes a gap between a claimed specialty and actual knowledge

base.update_signal: a renewal cycle's worth of evidence about whether each credential produced enquiries, access or knowledge the practice used

nodes.definition: Design how the client pays the practice, understanding that the choice reshapes the advisor's incentives more than it reshapes their income. The options in ordinary use are commission-only, where all revenue depends on the client booking something commissionable through the advisor; a professional or consultation fee charged before design work begins; a research or itinerary-design fee scaled to trip complexity; a per-booking service fee; a retainer for clients who travel repeatedly; and hybrids where a fee is credited against a subsequent booking. Each element needs four decisions written down: what work the fee buys and where that work stops, when it is charged relative to the design work, whether and how it is credited or refunded, and how it is explained in the first conversation. The alignment consequence is the real content: commission-only means the advisor is paid only if the client books, and paid differently depending on what they book, which is precisely the pressure that makes disclosure mandatory; a fee paid for advice decouples the advisor's income from which product is chosen and makes it possible to say honestly that a client should book direct, use points, or not take the trip at all. Fee charging can also interact with client-money and registration classes - verify that in your jurisdiction before launching a fee.

included: the fee instruments available and what each buys
timing, crediting and refund decisions
the incentive-alignment consequence of each option
the jurisdictional check that fee charging can trigger
excluded: how fees are invoiced and collected

pros.claim: A fee paid for advice lets the advisor recommend the option that is right even when it pays them nothing
pros.example: telling a client to use their own points for the flights and charging for the design work around them

pros.claim: Charging before design work filters out price-shoppers and protects the practice's scarcest asset, which is design time
pros.example: an enquiry that evaporates at the mention of a design fee, having intended to take the itinerary elsewhere

cons.claim: A fee adds friction at the exact moment a prospect is deciding whether to trust an advisor at all
cons.example: a first-time advisory client hesitating at paying before seeing anything, in a market where booking online costs nothing extra

cons.claim: Commission-only is easier to sell and, in some client communities, the only model that will be accepted
cons.example: a repeat cruise community that treats any planning fee as a reason to book elsewhere

failure_modes: charging a fee without being able to say in one sentence what it buys
quoting fees inconsistently across clients, which surfaces the moment two of them compare
adopting commission-only and then absorbing unlimited unpaid design work
launching a fee without checking whether taking client money triggers a registration or client-funds class
acceptance_tests: for each fee instrument the practice uses, the scope of work it buys, its timing, its crediting or refund rule and its one-sentence explanation are written and applied consistently
the fee schedule is stated to clients before any design work begins, never after
revisit_triggers: fee resistance clusters in a particular client type or enquiry source
design hours per trip drift far from what the fee assumed
a registration or client-funds requirement class that touches fee handling changes

base.update_signal: observed conversion and design-hour data by fee instrument across a season of real enquiries

nodes.definition: Operate a standing rule that the client is told how the advisor is paid and what relationships could tilt a recommendation, before they commit money. Begin with an inventory of every incentive that exists in this practice: commission that differs by supplier and by product category, preferred and consortium programme terms, production-tier improvements, supplier bonus or override offers, host split differences between product types, and hospitality such as familiarization travel and inspection stays. Then the rule set: disclose in writing, in plain words, that the practice earns supplier commission and any fees, and that it participates in preferred programmes; when a preferred or higher-paying option is recommended, present at least one credible alternative and record why the recommendation was made on the brief's terms; never let a compensation difference decide between two options unless the client has been told the difference exists; never describe a preferred relationship as an objective ranking or a best-available verdict; and never manufacture urgency or use fear about what could go wrong to move a decision. If a recommendation cannot be explained to the client in terms of their own stated brief, it is not a recommendation - it is steering, and it does not go out.

included: the incentive inventory
written compensation and programme disclosure before commitment
the alternative-and-rationale requirement
the anti-urgency and anti-fear rules

pros.claim: Written disclosure removes the worst outcome in an advisory relationship, which is a client discovering an undisclosed incentive later
pros.example: a client learning from a friend that the recommended property was a preferred partner and finding it was already stated in the engagement letter

pros.claim: Requiring an alternative and a written rationale disciplines the advisor's own thinking, not just the client's information
pros.example: an advisor noticing while writing the rationale that the preferred option does not actually fit the stated brief

cons.claim: Disclosure invites questions about compensation that consume trust-building time early in a relationship
cons.example: a first meeting spent explaining commission structure instead of the trip

cons.claim: Offering an alternative alongside every preferred recommendation lengthens proposals and can appear indecisive
cons.example: a client asking why the advisor cannot simply say which one is best

failure_modes: disclosing only when asked, or only after the client has committed
presenting a preferred supplier as an objective best without saying the relationship exists
letting a bonus or override quietly break a tie between two suitable options
using worry about what might go wrong as the lever that closes a decision
acceptance_tests: every client receives written compensation and programme disclosure before committing money, and the practice can show where it was sent
